```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = FALSE,
  comment = "",
  class.output = "spax-output",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 100
)
```

spax ships open data on general practice (GP) care in NHS Cornwall and the
Isles of Scilly, in south-west England, and the guides run on it. This page answers one
question: what is in the example data? It first shows the four ingredients
of every model in the two shapes spax takes, then introduces each object once:
what it holds, how the objects fit together and what they cannot tell you. By
the end you can load each one and build the inputs that the guides start from.
Nothing needs downloading. The `spax()` interface and the allocation model are
experimental and may change in later versions.

The page uses spax with terra for the grids, sf for the points and polygons,
and dplyr and ggplot2 for tables and maps.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

Four objects load with spax, and two grids are read from files:

| Object | What it holds | How to load it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `cornwall_gp` | `r nrow(cornwall_gp)` GP practices: location, GP workforce and list size | Loaded with spax |
| `cornwall_lsoa` | `r nrow(cornwall_lsoa)` small areas: boundaries, population and registered residents | Loaded with spax |
| `cornwall_flows` | Registered residents by small area and practice | Loaded with spax |
| `cornwall_travel` | Travel minutes from each small area to each practice | Loaded with spax |
| `cornwall_pop.tif` | Population grid of 30 arc-second cells | `read_spax_example()` |
| `cornwall_gp_travel.tif` | Travel minutes from each grid cell to each practice | `read_spax_example()` |

Each object has a help page with every column, for example `?cornwall_gp`.

## The four ingredients

Every model in spax uses four ingredients: **demand**, the people who need the
service; **supply**, what each facility offers; **travel**, the time from each
place to each facility; and, to fit the allocation model, **observed use**,
who uses which facility. spax takes them in two shapes:

| Ingredient | Table form (areas or points) | Grid form |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Demand | a number per origin | a population raster |
| Supply | a number per facility | the same |
| Travel | an origin x facility matrix of minutes (`Inf` = no connection) | one travel-time layer per facility |
| Observed use | flows (origin, facility, count) or facility totals | the same, with cells as origins |

The same models run on both shapes, and the example data hold both. In table
form, the origins are the small areas of `cornwall_lsoa` and the facilities the
practices of `cornwall_gp`; travel is `cornwall_travel` and observed use is
`cornwall_flows`. In grid form, demand is `cornwall_pop.tif` and travel is
`cornwall_gp_travel.tif`, for the same practices. In table form, each
ingredient is a vector or matrix named by ID. The code shows the first
elements of each.

```{r ingredients}
areas <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_lsoa)
gp <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)

# Demand: residents of each small area, named by its LSOA code
# (the allocation guides use its registered residents instead)
demand <- setNames(areas$pop, areas$lsoa)
head(demand, 4)

# Supply: GP FTE of each practice, named by its practice code
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
head(supply, 4)

# Travel: minutes from each small area (rows) to each practice (columns)
cornwall_travel[1:3, 1:4]

# Observed use: residents of each small area registered at each practice
head(cornwall_flows, 4)
```

In grid form, demand is one raster of residents per cell and travel a stack of
rasters with one layer per practice, named by practice code.
`read_spax_example()` reads both.

```{r ingredients-grids}
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")
```

The figure below draws the four ingredients on mainland Cornwall. To show
travel and observed use, it picks one practice of middle size.

```{r ingredients-practice}
# The practice drawn in panels (c) and (d)
chosen <- "L82004"
gp$name[gp$practice == chosen]
```

```{r ingredients-values, include = FALSE}
chosen_gp <- gp[gp$practice == chosen, ]
# Travel minutes from each mainland small area to that practice, from the
# matrix and from the grid cell under the area's centroid
mainland_areas <- areas[!areas$scilly, ]
matrix_minutes <- cornwall_travel[mainland_areas$lsoa, chosen]
grid_minutes <- extract(
  travel_grid[[chosen]],
  vect(mainland_areas, geom = c("cent_lon", "cent_lat"), crs = "EPSG:4326"),
  ID = FALSE
)[[1]]
# Share of each mainland area's registered residents registered there
at_chosen <- cornwall_flows[cornwall_flows$practice == chosen, ]
chosen_patients <- at_chosen$patients[match(mainland_areas$lsoa, at_chosen$lsoa)]
chosen_share <- ifelse(is.na(chosen_patients), 0, chosen_patients) / mainland_areas$registered
half_there <- chosen_share >= 0.5
# The text says the two forms agree for every area
stopifnot(all(matrix_minutes == grid_minutes))
```

It has `r round(chosen_gp$gp_fte_extg, 1)` GP FTE, against a median of
`r round(median(gp$gp_fte_extg), 1)` over all practices.

```{r ingredients-map, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = sprintf("Four maps of mainland Cornwall. (a) Demand: the population grid in residents per cell, in six classes, with the towns standing out, and the %d small-area centroids as circles sized by population. (b) Supply: the %d practices as orange circles sized by GP FTE. (c) Travel: minutes to %s as bands of 10, 20, 30 and 45 minutes from its travel-time layer, with the centroids as dots colored by the same bands from the travel matrix; the dots match the bands under them. (d) Observed use: the share of each small area's registered residents registered at that practice: at least half in %d areas around it, less in a ring beyond them and almost none in the rest of the county.", nrow(mainland_areas), sum(!gp$scilly), tools::toTitleCase(tolower(chosen_gp$name)), sum(half_there))}
# Mainland Cornwall as terra vectors, in the grids' longitude and latitude
mainland <- filter(cornwall_lsoa, !scilly)
outline <- vect(st_union(mainland))
area_polygons <- vect(mainland)
centroids <- vect(st_drop_geometry(mainland), geom = c("cent_lon", "cent_lat"), crs = "EPSG:4326")
practices <- vect(filter(cornwall_gp, !scilly))
chosen_point <- practices[practices$practice == chosen]

# Travel bands, in minutes, for the grid layer and the matrix column
bands <- c(0, 10, 20, 30, 45, 180)
band_colors <- hcl.colors(5, "YlOrRd")
minutes <- cornwall_travel[centroids$lsoa, chosen]

# Share of each area's registered residents registered at the practice
at_chosen <- filter(cornwall_flows, practice == chosen)
registered_there <- at_chosen$patients[match(area_polygons$lsoa, at_chosen$lsoa)]
area_polygons$share <- ifelse(is.na(registered_there), 0, registered_there) /
  area_polygons$registered

# Shared settings: the mainland window, margins, title size, legend at top left
window <- ext(outline)
margins <- c(0.2, 0.2, 1.2, 0.2)
title_size <- 0.85
legend_at <- list(x = "topleft", cex = 0.75)

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
# (a) Demand: the grid, and each small area at its centroid
plot(pop, ext = window, breaks = c(0, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 5000),
     col = hcl.colors(6, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE), axes = FALSE, mar = margins,
     cex.main = title_size, main = "(a) Demand: residents",
     plg = c(legend_at, title = "Per cell"))
lines(outline, lwd = 0.4)
points(centroids, cex = sqrt(centroids$pop / 3500), col = adjustcolor("grey10", 0.75), lwd = 0.6)

# (b) Supply: the practices
plot(outline, ext = window, col = "grey95", border = "grey40", lwd = 0.4, axes = FALSE,
     mar = margins, cex.main = title_size, main = "(b) Supply: GP FTE")
points(practices, cex = sqrt(practices$gp_fte_extg) / 1.5, pch = 21, bg = "orange")
legend("topleft", legend = c(2, 6, 12), title = "GP FTE", pch = 21, pt.bg = "orange",
       pt.cex = sqrt(c(2, 6, 12)) / 1.5, bty = "n", cex = 0.6, xpd = NA)

# (c) Travel: the practice's grid layer as bands, its matrix column as dots
plot(travel_grid[[chosen]], ext = window, breaks = bands, col = band_colors,
     axes = FALSE, mar = margins, cex.main = title_size,
     main = "(c) Travel: minutes to one practice", plg = c(legend_at, title = "Minutes"))
lines(outline, lwd = 0.4)
points(centroids, pch = 21, cex = 0.6, lwd = 0.4,
       bg = band_colors[findInterval(minutes, bands, left.open = TRUE)])
points(chosen_point, pch = 4, cex = 1.2, lwd = 2)

# (d) Observed use: the share registered at the practice
plot(area_polygons, "share", type = "interval", breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1),
     col = hcl.colors(5, "Blues", rev = TRUE), border = NA, ext = window, axes = FALSE,
     mar = margins, cex.main = title_size, main = "(d) Observed use: share registered there",
     plg = c(legend_at, title = "Share"))
lines(outline, lwd = 0.4)
points(chosen_point, pch = 4, cex = 1.2, lwd = 2)
par(op)
```

Panel (a) is demand in both shapes: the grid of residents per cell and, as
circles, the small areas at their centroids. Panel (b) is supply, the same in
both shapes. Panel (c) is travel to the practice, marked by the cross: the
bands are its layer of the travel stack, and the dots are its column of the
travel matrix, colored by the same bands. For each of the
`r length(matrix_minutes)` mainland small areas, the matrix gives the minutes
of the grid cell under the area's centroid, so each dot has the color of the
band beneath it. Panel (d) is observed use: in `r sum(half_there)` small
areas, all within `r max(matrix_minutes[half_there])` minutes of the practice,
between half and `r round(100 * max(chosen_share))`% of the registered
residents are registered there. Even next to it, some residents register
elsewhere, and in most of the county almost none register there. The
allocation model describes how such shares fall with travel time.

## Practices

`cornwall_gp` is an `sf` point layer in longitude and latitude (WGS 84,
EPSG:4326), one row per practice; `easting` and `northing` give the British
National Grid coordinates in meters. `practice` is the NHS practice code, which
links the practices to the registrations and to the travel times. The code
shows the first practices of `gp`, the table without its geometry.

```{r practices}
gp |>
  select(practice, name, gp_fte_extg, gp_fte, list_size) |>
  head()
```

The guides use `gp_fte_extg` as supply, what each practice offers: full-time
equivalent GPs (37.5 hours a week) excluding GPs in training, from the June
2026 workforce data. GPs in training are left out because they cluster in a
few training practices. `gp_fte` includes them. `list_size` counts all patients
registered at the practice. Each
practice sits at its main site, so branch surgeries do not appear.

## Small areas

`cornwall_lsoa` holds the `r nrow(cornwall_lsoa)` Lower layer Super Output
Areas (LSOA 2021) as polygons in longitude and latitude (WGS 84, like the
practices). Each area's population-weighted centroid is given twice: in
longitude and latitude (`cent_lon`, `cent_lat`) and in British National Grid
meters (`cent_x`, `cent_y`). The guides use longitude and latitude; the
British National Grid columns are kept for distances in meters and for joining
other UK data. The areas are small, of
`r format(min(cornwall_lsoa$pop), big.mark = ",")` to
`r format(max(cornwall_lsoa$pop), big.mark = ",")` residents. Each has an ONS
mid-2024 population estimate (`pop`, also by age band) and the number of its
residents registered at any GP practice in England (`registered`). That number
splits into residents registered at a practice in Cornwall and the Isles of
Scilly (`registered_in`) and those registered elsewhere (`registered_out`).
The code adds up these columns.

```{r small-areas}
c(
  population = sum(areas$pop),
  registered = sum(areas$registered),
  registered_in = sum(areas$registered_in),
  registered_out = sum(areas$registered_out)
)
```

`registered_in` and `registered_out` add up to `registered`. Registered
residents outnumber the population estimate by about
`r round(100 * (sum(areas$registered) / sum(areas$pop) - 1))`%, which reflects
list inflation (patients who stay on a list after moving away) and the
different reference dates. `ruc21` gives each area's rural-urban
classification (2021).

## Registrations

`cornwall_flows` counts the residents of each small area registered at each of
the `r nrow(cornwall_gp)` practices, one row per pair with at least one
registration; its first rows are printed above. The code checks that each
area's rows add up to its `registered_in`, and counts the pairs.

```{r flows}
# Each area's registrations add up to its registered_in
by_area <- tapply(cornwall_flows$patients, cornwall_flows$lsoa, sum)
all(by_area[areas$lsoa] == areas$registered_in)

c(
  pairs = nrow(cornwall_flows),
  registered_residents = sum(cornwall_flows$patients)
)
```

Every area's rows add up to its `registered_in`, so the flows hold all
`r format(sum(cornwall_flows$patients), big.mark = ",")` residents registered
inside Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, spread over
`r format(nrow(cornwall_flows), big.mark = ",")` area-practice pairs.

A registration is a **stock**: who is registered with which practice on one
date (July 2026), not a count of visits. Residents counted in
`registered_out` are registered with a practice outside Cornwall and the Isles
of Scilly, for example in Devon, so they are in `cornwall_lsoa` but not in
these flows. The guides on the allocation model, a model of where each area's
residents register, fit it to these counts. The guides on the accessibility
scores of the two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) family, which measure
supply per resident, do not use them.

## Travel times

`cornwall_travel` is a matrix of motorized travel minutes from each small
area's population-weighted centroid (rows, `cornwall_lsoa$lsoa`) to each
practice's main site (columns, `cornwall_gp$practice`); a corner of it is
printed above. The code summarizes the minutes from each area to its nearest
practice.

```{r travel}
# Minutes from each small area to its nearest practice
nearest <- apply(cornwall_travel, 1, min, na.rm = TRUE)
summary(nearest)
```

The times are least-cost paths over a 2019 global map of the time needed to
cross each 30 arc-second cell (a friction surface). They are rounded to whole
minutes, with a floor of one minute, so no time is 0.
`r sum(nearest == 1)` of the `r length(nearest)` small areas have a practice
at 1 minute. Traffic is not modeled. In towns several practices can share one
cell, so they have the same travel time from every area. The map shows the
time to the nearest practice.

```{r nearest-map, fig.alt = sprintf("Map of the small areas of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly colored by travel minutes to the nearest GP practice, from %d to %d minutes; most areas are within a few minutes of a practice, and the longest times are at the western tip, inland in the north-east and in one area on the north coast near Padstow.", min(nearest), max(nearest))}
# Join each area's nearest-practice time to its polygon
nearest_map <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  mutate(minutes = nearest[lsoa])

ggplot(nearest_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = minutes), color = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(cornwall_lsoa), fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Minutes", option = "magma", direction = -1) +
  labs(title = "Travel time to the nearest GP practice") +
  theme_void()
```

Most small areas are within a few minutes of a practice. The map gives most of
its area to the large rural areas, so the many small town areas, mostly at 1
minute, are hard to see. The longest trips, up to `r max(nearest)` minutes,
are at the western tip, inland in the north-east and in one area on the north
coast near Padstow.

## The grids

```{r cell-size, include = FALSE}
# Size of one cell at the middle of the grid: geodesic distances (WGS 84)
# between the middle point and the points one cell north and one cell east
cell_degrees <- res(pop)[1]
middle <- c(mean(ext(pop)[1:2]), mean(ext(pop)[3:4]))
corners <- vect(
  rbind(middle, middle + c(0, cell_degrees), middle + c(cell_degrees, 0)),
  crs = "EPSG:4326"
)
cell_km <- as.matrix(distance(corners))[2:3, 1] / 1000
```

Two GeoTIFF files, read above, cover the same grid in longitude and latitude.
Its cells are `r round(3600 * cell_degrees)` arc-seconds (1/`r round(1 / cell_degrees)`
degree) on each side; at Cornwall's latitude a cell is about
`r round(cell_km[1], 2)` km north-south by `r round(cell_km[2], 2)` km
east-west, or `r round(prod(cell_km), 2)` square km. `cornwall_pop.tif` holds
WorldPop 2020 estimated residents per cell: a **count**, not a density.
`cornwall_gp_travel.tif` holds one layer of travel minutes per practice, named
by practice code. The code counts their cells, layers and residents.

```{r grids}
c(
  cells = ncell(pop),
  populated_cells = sum(!is.na(values(pop))),
  travel_layers = nlyr(travel_grid),
  grid_residents = round(global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]),
  ons_residents = sum(areas$pop)
)
```

```{r grid-numbers, include = FALSE}
grid_total <- global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
grid_gap <- round(100 * (1 - grid_total / sum(areas$pop)))
cell_residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)
under_50 <- round(100 * mean(cell_residents[!is.na(cell_residents)] < 50))
```

The grid holds about `r grid_gap`% fewer residents than the ONS mid-2024
estimate in `cornwall_lsoa`. The two are different sources and dates: choose
one for an analysis and say which. In the travel layers, `NA` marks cells with
no residents, pairs with no road connection and journeys over 180 minutes.
Of the populated cells, `r under_50`% hold fewer than 50 residents; in panel
(a) of the figure above, the towns stand out with several hundred or more. The
guides on the 2SFCA family use the grid, and the allocation guides use the
registered residents of the small areas.

## The Isles of Scilly and the mainland

The Isles of Scilly have one small area and one practice, St Mary's Health
Centre (`L82017`). Road travel times cannot cross the sea, so every travel
time between the islands and the mainland is `NA`. The code counts the unknown
times in the small-area matrix.

```{r scilly}
c(
  unknown = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel)),
  scilly_area = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel[areas$scilly, ])),
  scilly_practice = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel[, gp$scilly]))
)
```

The unknown times are the Scilly area's row (to the `r sum(!gp$scilly)`
mainland practices) and the Scilly practice's column (from the
`r sum(!areas$scilly)` mainland areas). The islands do have access to the
mainland, by boat and air, which these travel times do not represent. Rather
than treat the islands as cut off, the guides model **mainland Cornwall
only**: `r sum(!areas$scilly)` small areas and `r sum(!gp$scilly)` practices,
selected with the `scilly` column. Mainland residents registered with the
Scilly practice or outside Cornwall then count as registered outside mainland
Cornwall. [Bringing your own data](data-prep.html) shows what the unknown
times do to an accessibility score when the islands are kept.

## The inputs used in the guides

The guides start from one of two short recipes, so that all of them model the
same mainland. Both prepare the data with `prep_data()`, which lines the
inputs up by ID for `spax()`, the function that runs a model on them.

[]{#a-grid-for-the-fca-indices}

### A grid, for the accessibility scores

A 2SFCA-family method gives each place an accessibility score: supply per
resident, counting nearby practices more than distant ones. The guides on the
2SFCA family compute it on the population grid and the travel stack. The
recipe keeps the mainland practices, then only the cells with a travel time to
every one of them, so that no populated cell has an unknown travel time.

```{r recipe-grid}
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
grid_data
```

`[[gp$practice]]` picks the travel layers of the mainland practices by name,
in the table's order. `sum(travel_grid)` is `NA` wherever any layer is `NA`,
so the mask keeps exactly the cells with complete travel. `trim()` drops the
empty margin the islands leave behind, and `crop()` cuts the travel stack to
the trimmed grid.

The mainland grid holds
`r format(round(global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]), big.mark = ",")`
residents, against `r format(round(grid_total), big.mark = ",")` in the full
grid. As the print says, `grid_data` points to the rasters rather than copying
them: run the recipe again in a new session instead of saving it.

### Small areas, for the allocation model

The allocation model gives each small area's residents a probability of
registering at each practice, or with the outside option: a practice outside
the data. It runs on numeric inputs named by ID: demand (the people of each
small area who may register), supply by practice and the travel matrix
between them. Demand is the registered residents of each area, so it counts
the same people as the registrations. The mainland rows and columns of
`cornwall_travel` have no unknown times. The labels in `metadata` record units
and dates with the data. spax keeps them with every result and does not
convert them.

```{r recipe-areas}
areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")
d
flows
```

```{r outside-gap, include = FALSE}
at_mainland <- cornwall_flows$lsoa %in% areas$lsoa &
  cornwall_flows$practice %in% gp$practice
outside_gap <- sum(areas$registered) - sum(cornwall_flows$patients[at_mainland])
```

`d` holds `r nrow(areas)` small areas (origins) by `r nrow(gp)` practices
(facilities), all active, that is, with demand above zero. Their demand is
larger than their registrations at mainland practices by
`r format(outside_gap, big.mark = ",")` residents: those registered elsewhere,
whom the outside option stands for. The `policies` line records what `d` does
with missing demand and unknown travel: here both are errors, and there are
none. [Bringing your own
data](data-prep.html#inputs-for-the-allocation-model) shows the other
choices. `flows` names its loss, Poisson, which is how a fit compares modeled
with observed counts.

`obs_flows()` declares the observed registrations from the long table, which
still includes the Isles of Scilly. When `spax()` fits a model, it matches the
counts to the data and says in a message which counts it sets aside.
[Bringing your own data](data-prep.html#observed-counts-in-a-long-table)
explains that message.

## Sources, dates and licenses

| Data | Objects | Source and date | License |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Registrations | `cornwall_gp`, `cornwall_lsoa`, `cornwall_flows` | NHS England, Patients Registered at a GP Practice, July 2026 | Open Government Licence v3.0 |
| GP workforce | `cornwall_gp` | NHS England, General Practice Workforce, 30 June 2026 | Open Government Licence v3.0 |
| Practice locations | `cornwall_gp` | ONS Postcode Directory, November 2025 | Open Government Licence v3.0; contains OS and Royal Mail data |
| Boundaries, centroids, population | `cornwall_lsoa` | ONS LSOA 2021 boundaries and rural-urban classification, population-weighted centroids, mid-2024 population estimates | Open Government Licence v3.0; contains OS data |
| Population grid | `cornwall_pop.tif` | WorldPop, 2020 UN-adjusted estimates on a 30 arc-second grid | Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 |
| Travel times | `cornwall_travel`, `cornwall_gp_travel.tif` | Derived by the package author from the Malaria Atlas Project 2019 motorized friction surface (Weiss et al. 2020) | Creative Commons Attribution (version 3.0 on the Malaria Atlas Project website, 4.0 in the Google Earth Engine catalogue; both permit sharing adapted data with attribution) |

Each source keeps the license given in the table. The package's MIT license
covers its code only. The registrations and the workforce are from 2026, the
population grid from 2020, the small-area
population from mid-2024 and the road network from about 2019, so keep the
dates in mind when reading results. The full attributions, with the required
wording for each source, are installed with the package:

```{r copyrights, eval = FALSE}
file.show(system.file("COPYRIGHTS", package = "spax"))
```

  model to these registrations.

  option and the accessibility scores can and cannot tell you.
